prompt: The section compares an electron's spin and orbital angular momenta to two motions of the Earth. Which motion of the Earth is spin like?

choices.text: Its daily turning about its own axis
Its yearly orbit around the Sun
choices.why: The annual orbit around the Sun matches orbital angular momentum. Spin matches the Earth's daily turning about its own axis.

choices.text: The Moon's monthly orbit around it
choices.why: The analogy uses only the Earth's own two motions. Spin is like its daily turning, and orbital angular momentum like its annual orbit.

choices.text: The slow wobble of its tilted axis in space
choices.why: The analogy doesn't use the wobble. Spin is likened to the Earth's daily rotation, and orbital motion to its yearly trip around the Sun.

explanation: Spin and orbital angular momentum are analogous to the Earth's daily and annual motions, respectively. Spin is like the Earth turning on its own axis; orbital angular momentum is like its orbit around the Sun.

prompt: According to the section, what is the spin of an electron?

choices.text: An intrinsic angular momentum it always has
The angular momentum of its orbit about a nucleus
choices.why: That is orbital angular momentum. Spin is a separate, intrinsic angular momentum that the electron has in addition to any orbital motion.

choices.text: Angular momentum it gains only in a magnetic field
choices.why: Spin is intrinsic, so the electron always has it, field or no field.

choices.text: A property that no other particle shares
choices.why: The section says certain other fundamental particles also possess spin, so it isn't unique to the electron.

explanation: The electron possesses an intrinsic angular momentum, or spin, in addition to its orbital angular momentum. Certain other fundamental particles have spin too.

prompt: To keep spin apart from orbital angular momentum, which quantum numbers does the section use for spin in place of ℓ and m?

choices.text: s and m_s
n and ℓ
choices.why: n and ℓ describe an orbital's size and shape. For spin, the section uses s and m_s in place of ℓ and m.

choices.text: j and m_j
choices.why: j and m_j label total angular momentum, not spin alone. The section's spin quantum numbers are s and m_s.

choices.text: ℓ and m, as for orbitals
choices.why: The section introduces new symbols precisely to tell spin apart from orbital angular momentum: s and m_s.

explanation: Spin quantum numbers are written s and m_s, in place of the ℓ and m used for orbital angular momentum. They play matching roles: s fixes the size of the spin, and m_s its component along z.

prompt: For an electron, how do the spin quantum numbers s and m_s differ?

choices.text: s is always 1/2; m_s is +1/2 or −1/2
s is +1/2 or −1/2; m_s is always 1/2
choices.why: That swaps them. s has the single value 1/2 for every electron, while m_s takes one of two values, ±1/2.

choices.text: s is always 1; m_s is +1, 0 or −1
choices.why: The electron's s is 1/2, not 1, so m_s has only the two values +1/2 and −1/2.

choices.text: Both are always exactly 1/2
choices.why: Only s is fixed at 1/2. m_s can be +1/2 or −1/2, which gives the electron its two spin states.

explanation: For the electron, s always has the value 1/2, which is why it is called a particle of spin 1/2. m_s can take one of two values, +1/2 or −1/2.

prompt: Besides the electron, which particles does the section say have spin 1/2?

choices.text: The proton and the neutron
The photon and the proton
choices.why: The photon has integer spin, which makes it a boson. The proton and neutron have spin 1/2, like the electron.

choices.text: The photon and the neutron
choices.why: The photon has integer spin, not spin 1/2. The particles named with spin 1/2 are the proton and the neutron.

choices.text: None; only the electron has spin 1/2
choices.why: The section names the proton and the neutron as spin-1/2 particles too, along with the electron.

explanation: The proton and neutron also have spin 1/2. Like the electron, they are fermions, governed by the Pauli exclusion principle.

prompt: According to the section, why can an arbitrary number of photons occupy the same quantum state?

choices.text: They are bosons, not bound by the Pauli principle
They are fermions, which obey the Pauli principle
choices.why: Obeying the Pauli principle is exactly what stops fermions from sharing a state. Photons have integer spin, so they are bosons.

choices.text: They have spin 1/2, just like electrons do
choices.why: Spin-1/2 particles such as electrons are fermions and can't share a state. Photons have integer spin, which makes them bosons.

choices.text: They have no spin, so states don't limit them
choices.why: Photons do have spin: an integer value. That makes them bosons, which don't obey the Pauli principle.

explanation: Photons have integer spin and are classified as bosons. Bosons do not obey the Pauli principle, so an arbitrary number of them can occupy the same quantum state.

prompt: The section classifies the neutron as a fermion. At most how many identical neutrons can occupy the same quantum state?
explanation: Fermions are governed by the Pauli exclusion principle, so no two identical fermions can share a quantum state: the most is 1. Bosons, such as photons, have no such limit.

prompt: A complete theory of spin requires relativistic quantum mechanics. According to the section, what is enough for our purposes?

choices.text: Recognizing the electron's two internal states
Working through the full relativistic theory
choices.why: The section says the complete relativistic theory isn't needed here. It is enough to recognize the two internal states, spin up and spin down.

choices.text: Picturing the electron as a tiny spinning ball
choices.why: The section offers no spinning-ball picture. It asks only that we recognize the electron's two internal states, spin up and spin down.

choices.text: Leaving spin out, since it barely affects atoms
choices.why: Spin can't be left out: the section says spins play an essential role in determining the electronic states of atoms and molecules.

explanation: For our purposes, it is enough to recognize the two possible internal states of the electron, spin up and spin down. The full theory of spin needs relativistic quantum mechanics.

prompt: How does the section bring the electron's spin up and spin down states into its wavefunction?

choices.text: As α and β factors in the wavefunction
As α and β terms added to the wavefunction
choices.why: α and β multiply the rest of the wavefunction as factors; they aren't added on as separate terms.

choices.text: As a + or − sign on the whole wavefunction
choices.why: Spin isn't shown by a sign. Spin up and spin down are written as the factors α and β in the wavefunction.

choices.text: As extra values of the quantum number ℓ
choices.why: ℓ belongs to orbital angular momentum. The two spin states enter as the factors α and β.

explanation: Spin up and spin down are designated α and β, respectively, and enter the electron wavefunction as factors. A one-electron wavefunction is then a spatial part times α or β.

prompt: According to the section, what do spins play an essential role in determining?

choices.text: The possible electronic states of atoms
The masses of atoms and molecules
choices.why: Spin doesn't set mass. The section says spins help determine the possible electronic states of atoms and molecules.

choices.text: The sizes and shapes of atomic orbitals
choices.why: Orbital sizes and shapes come from n and ℓ. Spins instead help decide which electronic states atoms and molecules can have.

choices.text: The number of protons in each nucleus
choices.why: The proton count is the atomic number, which spin doesn't change. Spins help determine the possible electronic states of atoms and molecules.

explanation: Spins play an essential role in determining the possible electronic states of atoms and molecules. For example, two electrons can share an orbital only if their spins are opposite.
